lessons.title: Figma UI Design Course: A Beginners Tutorial
objectives: Distinguish what UI is from what UX is
Set up a file with frames that match a real device
Judge a design by the phone it will be used on
lessons.notes:
UX is deciding what the thing should do and in what order. UI is how it looks and how it is touched. Module 3 covers the first properly; this module is the second, and the tool that does it.

THE MENTAL MODEL IN FIGMA: an infinite canvas holding FRAMES. A frame is a screen. Inside frames are layers - shapes, text, images - and frames can sit inside frames, which is how a card inside a screen works. Everything else in the tool is a way of arranging those.

START EVERY FILE WITH THE RIGHT FRAME SIZE, because designing on the wrong canvas produces work that has to be redone. The preset sizes are a starting point and not a decision.

THE FOUR THINGS THAT MAKE A SCREEN LOOK DESIGNED RATHER THAN ASSEMBLED, and they are worth more than any plugin: CONSISTENT SPACING using a repeating unit such as eight, so gaps are 8, 16, 24 rather than whatever was dragged; A TYPE SCALE of three or four sizes rather than eleven; A SMALL PALETTE, one main colour plus neutrals; and ALIGNMENT, because most amateur screens are simply not aligned.

WHITE SPACE IS NOT WASTED SPACE. Crowding is the commonest beginner mistake and the easiest to fix.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - design for the phone your user actually holds. Tutorials design on a large recent handset, and the result is a portfolio piece that fails in the market you are designing for. MOST USERS HERE ARE ON A MID-RANGE OR OLDER ANDROID with a smaller screen, so check your screen at a narrower width and with the system font scaled up, which many people set because they are reading outdoors. CONTRAST MATTERS MORE THAN IT DOES IN A TUTORIAL, because a cheap screen in Nairobi sunlight loses everything subtle - pale grey text on white is invisible on a boda at midday. And remember that WEIGHT IS A DESIGN DECISION: every large image and custom font you add costs the user money on a bundle, so a designer who reaches for three typefaces and a hero video has made a financial decision on someone else's behalf.
lessons.practice: Rebuild one screen of an app you use daily, at a narrower frame width than the preset. Use an eight-unit spacing scale, four type sizes and one main colour. Then view it at arm's length in bright light and fix everything you cannot read.

quiz.question: What is the difference between UI and UX?
options: UX decides what it does and in what order; UI is how it looks and is touched
UI is for apps, UX is for websites
UX is research, UI is prototyping
They are two names for the same work

quiz.question: Why is adding three typefaces and a hero video a design decision with a cost?
options: Weight costs the user money on a data bundle
It slows down the Figma file
It limits which plugins work
It makes the file harder to hand over

lessons.title: Figma Tutorial For Beginners
objectives: Move confidently around the Figma interface
Organise a file so someone else can open it
Work within the free tier on the machine you have
lessons.notes:
This is the mechanics lesson. Have Figma open and rebuild what the video builds - watching it is not learning it.

WHAT YOU ACTUALLY NEED TO KNOW: creating frames, drawing shapes, placing and masking images, text, the layers panel, groups, and the right-hand panel where size, position, fill, stroke and effects live. That is most of the tool.

THE LAYERS PANEL IS THE FILE. A file where every layer is called Rectangle 47 is a file nobody else can work in, including you next month. Name things as you make them - it costs seconds and saves hours.

ORGANISE FROM THE START: one page for wireframes, one for the real screens, one for scraps you are not ready to delete. Name frames after the screen they are - Home, Product, Checkout - not Frame 12.

SHARING: Figma runs in a browser and a link is the file. Share for viewing when someone only needs to look and commenting when you want feedback, and keep editing to people who are genuinely working on it.

THE FREE TIER is generous and it has limits on how many editable files a team can hold and how much version history is kept. Know where the limit is before a client is depending on the file.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - making Figma workable on the equipment and connection people here actually have. It is demanding on an older laptop, so KEEP FILES SMALL: one project per file rather than a year of work in one, compress images before placing them, and delete the pages you are no longer using. A heavy file is slow for you and worse for a client opening it on a phone. WORK WITH THE DESKTOP APP if your browser struggles, and expect that a poor connection shows up as saving delays rather than as an error - check that your last change is really saved before closing. And when you send a client a link, SEND A SPECIFIC FRAME rather than the whole file: clients open a crowded canvas, cannot find the screen, and give you feedback on an old version.
lessons.practice: Rebuild the tutorial file yourself, naming every layer and frame as you go. Organise it into wireframe, design and scrap pages. Then share a link to one specific frame with someone as a commenter, and ask them to find the thing you wanted feedback on without any explanation.

quiz.question: Why name layers as you create them?
options: A file of Rectangle 47 layers is unusable by anyone, including you next month
It reduces the file size
It is required for prototyping
Plugins need named layers

quiz.question: How should you send a design to a client?
options: A link to the specific frame, since a crowded canvas produces feedback on old versions
A link to the whole file
An exported image only
A downloaded copy of the file

lessons.title: Figma Wireframe Tutorial For Beginners
objectives: Use wireframes to get useful feedback early
lessons.notes:
A wireframe is the plan of a screen - what is on it, how important each thing is, and where it sits - deliberately drawn in grey boxes so nobody discusses the colour yet.

WHY LOW FIDELITY IS THE POINT. Two reasons, and both are practical. You can throw away an hour of grey boxes; you cannot throw away two days of polished screens, so you defend them instead. And a client shown a finished-looking design comments on the logo and the blue, while the same client shown grey boxes talks about whether the steps are right - which is the conversation you actually need.

WHAT A WIREFRAME MUST DECIDE: what this screen is for, the one thing the user should do on it, the hierarchy of everything else, and what happens next. If it does not answer those, adding colour will not save it.

START FROM THE FLOW, not the screen. Module 3 covered user flows; the wireframe is one step of that flow made concrete. Drawing beautiful screens with no flow behind them is the commonest way to waste a week.

KEEP IT PLAIN: grey boxes, a cross for an image, real words for labels rather than placeholder text, since fake text hides the fact that your button label makes no sense.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - wireframe the states everyone forgets, because they are most of the real experience here. Tutorials wireframe the happy path only. You need: LOADING, which on a slow bundle is not a flicker but several seconds a user will stare at; EMPTY, the screen before any data exists, which is the first thing a new user sees and is usually designed last; FAILED, because connection drops mid-action here as a matter of routine, and the screen must say what failed and offer a retry rather than silently reverting; and OFFLINE, which is a normal condition rather than an edge case. A design that handles those four is worth more than one that is beautiful on the happy path, and drawing them is cheap while everything is still grey boxes.
lessons.practice: Take one flow of three screens and wireframe it in grey boxes with real words, no colour. Then wireframe the four states for the main screen - loading, empty, failed and offline. Show the set to someone and note whether they discuss the steps rather than the styling.

quiz.question: Why show a client grey boxes rather than a polished screen?
options: They discuss whether the steps are right instead of the logo and the colour
It is faster to produce
It hides unfinished work
Polished screens cannot be printed

quiz.question: Which states do tutorials usually skip?
options: Loading, empty, failed and offline
Success and confirmation
Onboarding and settings
Search and filter

lessons.title: Prototyping in Figma | How to Prototype in Figma?
objectives: Turn static screens into something a person can tap through
Test a prototype with a real user and learn from it
Prototype only the path you need to answer a question
lessons.notes:
A prototype connects screens so someone can move through them. It turns a design from something you explain into something a person uses, and that difference is where you find out whether it works.

THE MECHANICS: connect an element on one frame to another frame, choose the interaction (a tap) and the transition. Keep transitions plain - an elaborate animation in a prototype is a distraction from the question you are asking.

PROTOTYPE THE PATH, NOT THE PRODUCT. Wiring every button on every screen takes days and answers nothing extra. Connect the one journey you need to test - find the item, add it, pay, done - and leave the rest.

TESTING IT IS THE POINT, and it is simpler than people expect. Give the phone to someone who has not seen it, give them a task in their own words - buy the blue one - and then SAY NOTHING. Watch where they hesitate. Every time you want to explain something, write it down instead: that is a design problem you just found.

FIVE PEOPLE IS ENOUGH to find most of the serious problems. You do not need a laboratory or a budget, and you do not need designers - you need people like your actual users.

WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR: hesitation, taps on things that are not buttons, going back, and asking you a question. Not whether they like it.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - two things that make this real here. TEST ON A PHONE, IN THE HAND, not on your laptop screen. Open the prototype on a mid-range Android, outdoors if that is where it will be used, and hand it over. Thumbs cover half the screen, glare kills contrast, and a target that was obvious on a laptop is missed three times. Second, PROTOTYPE THE PAYMENT HANDOFF HONESTLY: an M-Pesa payment takes the user out of your app to a prompt and back again, which is a real break in the journey, and the screen they return to must tell them clearly whether it worked, what to do if the prompt never came, and how to check without paying twice. Almost no international tutorial designs that moment, and it is the one where real users here abandon a purchase.
lessons.practice: Prototype one journey only, end to end, with plain transitions - including the payment handoff and the screen the user returns to. Open it on a mid-range phone and give it to five people with a task in their own words. Say nothing, write down every hesitation, and fix the three that appeared most.

quiz.question: What should you do while someone tests your prototype?
options: Say nothing, and write down every explanation you wanted to give
Guide them through the first screen
Ask whether they like the design
Explain what each button does

quiz.question: Why prototype the M-Pesa handoff?
options: The user leaves the app and returns, and that return screen is where purchases are abandoned
It is required for testing
It shortens the journey
Prototypes cannot show external screens

lessons.title: Build It in Figma: Create a Design System — Components
objectives: Assemble reusable styles and components into a small system
Name things so another person can use them
Judge when a design system is worth building
lessons.notes:
Module 4 covered components and variants. A design system is those, organised and named, plus the decisions that sit underneath them - the colours, the type sizes, the spacing - written down so every screen uses the same ones.

WHAT TO BUILD, in this order and no other:
COLOUR STYLES first, and few. A main colour, a neutral range from near-black to near-white, and three status colours for success, warning and error. Name them by ROLE rather than by appearance - primary, surface, text-muted - because a style named blue-500 is a problem the day the brand changes.
TYPE STYLES next, three or four sizes with their weights and line heights fixed.
SPACING, as a repeating unit.
THEN COMPONENTS: button with its variants, input field with its states, card, navigation bar. Build the ones you have already drawn twice.

THE STATES ARE THE WHOLE VALUE of a component. A button is not one thing - it is default, pressed, disabled and loading. Designing all four once, inside the component, is what stops the disabled state being invented differently on every screen.

DOCUMENT IT LIGHTLY: one page showing each component with a line saying when to use it. Without that, another designer guesses, and the system decays in a fortnight.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the judgement that saves you weeks. A DESIGN SYSTEM IS OVERKILL FOR A FIVE-SCREEN PROJECT. For a small job, colour and type styles plus two or three components is the whole benefit; the rest is enjoyable work that the client does not need and cannot maintain. Build the full thing when several people work on it, or when the product will keep growing. Two local points on the content: include a LOADING AND AN OFFLINE STATE in the components themselves, because on this market's connections they are used constantly and inventing them per screen guarantees inconsistency. And check every colour pair for CONTRAST IN SUNLIGHT ON A CHEAP SCREEN rather than trusting how it looks on your laptop - the muted grey that reads beautifully indoors disappears outside, which is where a great many of your users are.
lessons.practice: Build the small version: colour styles named by role, four type styles, a spacing unit, and three components with every state including loading and disabled. Document each on one page with a line on when to use it. Then apply the system to two existing screens and note everything it forced you to change.

quiz.question: Why name a colour style by role rather than appearance?
options: A style named blue-500 becomes a problem the day the brand changes
Role names are shorter
Appearance names break plugins
It groups them alphabetically

quiz.question: When is a full design system not worth building?
options: On a five-screen project, where styles and two or three components give the whole benefit
When the client has no brand
When working alone
When the deadline is more than a month away

lessons.title: Fully Responsive Website Design in Figma
objectives: Design one layout that works across screen sizes
Use constraints and auto layout to make resizing predictable
Decide what changes and what is dropped at each size
lessons.notes:
Responsive design means one design that reorganises itself for the screen it is on, rather than three separate designs that drift apart.

THE MECHANISM in Figma is constraints and auto layout, which Module 4 introduced. Constraints say what an element does when its frame changes - pinned to the left, stretched, centred. Auto layout makes a frame arrange its children and resize around them. Between them, a properly built component resizes without being redrawn.

DESIGN THE NARROW ONE FIRST. Starting wide and squeezing down forces you to decide what to throw away, and everything feels like a compromise. Starting narrow forces you to decide what genuinely matters, and then widening is a pleasure. This is not a stylistic preference - it produces better decisions.

THREE SIZES ARE ENOUGH for most work: a phone, a tablet-ish middle, and a desktop. More than that is usually someone designing for devices rather than for content.

WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGES between sizes: the number of columns, whether navigation is visible or behind a menu, image sizes, and how much supporting text you show. WHAT SHOULD NOT CHANGE: the order of importance. If the phone shows the price first, the desktop should not bury it.

TEST BY DRAGGING THE FRAME EDGE. If things pile up or overlap, your constraints are wrong - fix them rather than nudging elements into place, because the nudge will not survive the next change.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - narrow-first is not a preference in this market, it is the requirement. THE OVERWHELMING MAJORITY OF VISITS HERE ARE ON A PHONE, often an older one with a small screen, so the phone layout is the design and the desktop one is the variation. Design it at a narrower width than the fashionable preset. Keep TAP TARGETS GENEROUS, because thumbs are imprecise and people are often walking or in a matatu. And be ruthless about WEIGHT at every size: a hero image that looks magnificent on a desktop mockup is a slow, expensive page on a bundle, so specify compressed images, and be prepared to tell a client that the full-screen video they asked for will cost them visitors.
lessons.practice: Take one page and design it at a narrow phone width first, then widen it to a middle and a desktop size using constraints and auto layout only - no redrawing. Drag the frame edge across every width and fix whatever piles up. Then write down what you dropped at the narrow size and whether the order of importance stayed the same.

quiz.question: Why design the narrow layout first?
options: It forces you to decide what genuinely matters, rather than what to throw away
Phone frames are quicker to draw
Desktop layouts cannot use auto layout
Clients prefer to see phones first

quiz.question: Elements pile up when you drag the frame edge. What is wrong?
options: The constraints - fix those rather than nudging elements into place
The frame size preset
The auto layout spacing value
The image resolution
